quote: What interested you in solar? Saving some money?
stewart_read: The rep asks the anchor interest question but immediately supplies his own answer, which both leads the witness and short-circuits the depth this item is designed to capture.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep could be using a warm-up guess to prompt an easier answer from a possibly shy customer.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to ask the interest question open-ended and let silence sit — the customer's real answer (pool heater) came right after, unprompted, showing the guess wasn't needed.

quote: Yeah. We wanna get a pool heater, but we wanted to to, run it off solar.
stewart_read: Pool heater plan signals a planned increase in electric load — exactly the kind of usage-growth signal that should sharpen system sizing and justify urgency, but the rep only echoes the words back mechanically.
coaching_implication: Flag this as a walked-past enthusiasm signal. The rep should have anchored on it explicitly ('so we'll want to size the system with that pool heater load in mind') to make the appointment feel personalized and to flag it for the closer.

quote: And do you guys have, like, like, generators for the solar panels?
stewart_read: Customer asks a legitimate specialist-tier question about battery/backup options.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep could be seen as correctly deferring since he does redirect to the specialist.
coaching_implication: The redirect itself was correct in principle but delivered so haltingly ('We have batteries that we might have generators... I'm basically, I'm just building design') that it undercuts credibility; coach a clean, confident version of the universal escape hatch line.

quote: We have batteries that we might have generators. You can talk to the so I'm basically, I'm just building design, so you talk to the specialist.
stewart_read: The line is riddled with hedges and false starts ('might have', 'basically', restart mid-sentence), which reads as uncertain rather than a deliberate scope-hold.
alternative_hypothesis: This could simply be a transcription artifact of natural speech rather than a genuine confidence issue.
coaching_implication: Replay this clip with the rep — the content of the redirect is right, but the delivery needs to be tightened into one clean sentence to sound authoritative.

quote: It says it's two thousand three sixty.
stewart_read: Customer supplies a concrete kWh usage figure — the exact anchor point the schema calls for — and the rep neither acknowledges nor flips it, moving straight to confirming photo receipt.
coaching_implication: This is the clearest missed flip on the call. Coach the rep to respond to a number like this with a reflection ('that's a solid amount of usage, especially once that pool heater's running') rather than silence.

quote: Okay. I so you're in Richmond? That's your that's what you're assigned to?
stewart_read: Rep visibly works out territory/team assignment live on the call, including uncertainty about which day the local team meets, which is an internal operational fumble surfaced to the customer.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be seen as harmless transparency rather than a competence problem.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to do territory lookup silently or with a brief 'let me pull up your team' rather than narrating the uncertainty live, which can read as disorganized.

quote: K. I'll get working on your design, and then we'll see you on Monday.
stewart_read: The call closes without the full button-up: no one-hour block statement, no no-driving/computer instruction, no explicit text-follow-up promise, and no 'is that fair?' handshake.
alternative_hypothesis: The appointment day and time were locked (09:30 Monday the 23rd), so the core booking mechanic is intact even though the full button-up script wasn't run.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to run the full button-up checklist even on short, cooperative calls — the missing no-driving/computer instruction and hour-block framing are tied to no-show rate per schema.
